text: Teginabad was not a city pretending to be one. It was a wall, a gate, and the men who stood in it - a fortress squatting on patterned brick where the Ghazni road narrowed toward the desert crossing beyond. After the capital's crowded lanes, the outpost felt like a held breath. Farrukh's caravan guide reined in a full bowshot before the gate, the way a man slows before knocking on a door he isn't sure will open.

text: A man came out to meet them before they'd finished dismounting - young for the {{amid|amid}} he claimed, his robe good cloth gone thin at the cuffs, the particular tiredness of someone paid to want more from travelers than they wished to give. He named himself Sa'id ibn Yaqub, amid of the Teginabad customs post, and asked, with the practiced patience of a man who has asked it a thousand times, to see the manifest.

text: He did not ask unkindly. That, Farrukh would learn, was almost worse - Sa'id had the manner of a man doing arithmetic in his head at all times, converting every traveler into a quota he owed someone above him, and that someone into a quota owed to Ghazni, and Ghazni, lately, into a court nervous about a frontier that kept sending back worse news than it sent revenue. "They tell us collect what Nasa isn't sending anymore," he said, not quite to Farrukh, checking a seal against a wax impression in his own ledger. "As if a customs post can tax a rumor."

text: He found the discrepancy the way men who have found a thousand discrepancies find them - without surprise, only a faint, professional interest. The {{ushr|'ushr}} was already logged and paid; that was never in question. This was a different matter: a weight of silk logged as originating from a house in Rayy that no merchant road from Ghazni to Teginabad had any business touching. "Interesting bill of lading, this," Sa'id said, not looking up. "I'll need to open the crates."

text: The call to {{zuhr|midday prayer}} rose from the post's small mosque before Farrukh could answer him - the {{adhan|adhan}}, unhurried, indifferent to customs disputes. Sa'id closed his ledger at the sound the way another man might close a door. "God's business first," he said, and went, leaving Farrukh standing in the yard with the crates still sealed and the whole caravan's fate apparently subordinate to the sun's position in the sky. Farrukh did not pray, not then - grief had made his prayers thin and mechanical since Ghazni, words without the man behind them believing they reached anywhere - but he found himself doing the other thing the old letter-writer had given him instead: counting what in this moment was borrowed and what, if anything, was his. The crates were not his - his father's, or his father's creditors', depending on which qadi you asked, though none had asked. The debt was his, by his own mouth, at a graveside, to no one's compulsion. Perhaps that was the one contingent thing a man got to choose for himself: not what he was given, but what he agreed to carry.

text: Sa'id returned unhurried, prayer's calm still on him, and made Farrukh an offer with the same flat patience he'd made every other statement: the inspection could happen, properly, crate by crate, manifest against goods - a process that would take the rest of the day and might, Sa'id did not pretend otherwise, turn up exactly the kind of irregularity that got shipments impounded and merchants questioned by men less patient than himself. Or the post's fee for "expedited passage" could be settled now, quietly, and the caravan could be through the gate before the sun moved another hand's width.

text: Farrukh paid it. He told himself, counting the coins into Sa'id's palm, that this was arithmetic and nothing else - the same arithmetic Sa'id himself was always doing, obligation converted to obligation, all the way up to a Sultan who'd never see a dirham of it and all the way down to a father's debt Farrukh was still, by his own word, carrying. It did not feel like arithmetic. It felt like the first small dishonesty of the man he might become on this road, and he could not yet tell if that was a cost or simply a toll, the same as any other.

text: Farrukh let him look. Sa'id's men worked through the crates with the bored thoroughness of soldiers who had done this a hundred times and expected the hundred-and-first to be exactly as dull - until one of them went still over an unmarked bolt of cloth, and unwound from inside it not more cloth but a flat leather packet, sewn shut, no house mark anywhere on it. Sa'id crouched to look himself, cut the stitching open with a thumbnail, and tipped out a handful of unstamped silver counters and a strip of parchment scored with marks that matched no script Farrukh had ever been taught to read. He did not immediately say what he made of it.

text: "There was a second paper," Farrukh said, before he'd decided to say it - the same way he'd once stepped forward at a grave. "Unsigned. My father's clerk wouldn't finish reading it aloud." Sa'id looked up at him for a long moment, weighing something that had nothing to do with customs law. "Then you already know more than I do," he said, "which is not usually true of the men I stop at this gate." He did not write anything further in his ledger that day.

text: The caravan guide who'd brought them from Ghazni collected his fee at the gate and turned back the way they'd come - his contract, like the road behind them, ended at Teginabad. Farrukh spent what remained of the afternoon doing the ordinary, unglamorous work of the road: asking after a caravan master bound for Bost who'd take on a smaller party, haggling nothing, since there was nothing left in him to haggle with, and simply agreeing to the first honest face that offered a fair arrangement - a decision he suspected his father would have made faster, and better, and made anyway.

text: Teginabad's gate stood ahead of him now in the last honest light of the day, patterned brick walls he would pass through once and not again, Sa'id already back at his post, a man who would forget Farrukh's face by nightfall and remember, if he remembered anything, only the shipment's strange manifest. Beyond the gate, the road to Bost ran through country that still, for one more year, called itself Ghaznavid without irony. Farrukh did not know yet how short a lease that word had left. He knew only that the debt was still his, the letter's secret still unresolved, and that somewhere ahead, his father's actual road - not the one Nasuh's ledger recorded, but the one the man had actually walked - was still waiting to be found. First, though, there was the ordinary business of leaving properly provisioned.

text: At the last stall before the gate closed off the desert road, a woman was calling out prices for waterskins, dried dates, and feed enough for two animals across empty country - the same unglamorous arithmetic Farrukh had waved past an hour before, when the caravan master's fee hadn't seemed worth arguing over. This time, for no reason he could have named, it did. She named eight dirhams for the lot, in the flat voice of someone who'd already decided what she'd settle for and wasn't going to say so first.

text: She didn't look up from tying off a waterskin. "Eight is the price for a man who wants to reach Bost with feed left over," she said. "I can do seven, if you're the praying kind and don't mind your animals thinking hard thoughts about you around Bost." It wasn't much of a concession. It was, Farrukh noted with something almost like satisfaction, a concession.

"My son's posted out past Nasa," she said, following his glance without being asked, in the same flat voice she'd named every price in. "Garrison pay doesn't always find him out there anymore, not since the roads got the way they've gotten. text: Farrukh's guide, hearing where the provisioner's son was posted, allowed that the stretch ahead deserved the reputation Ghazni gave it - heat that would press down rather than simply exist, a horizon that would give back the same flat, colorless nothing for most of a day at a stretch, and watchposts strung along it whose pay reached them a good deal less reliably than the men holding them deserved, by everything the guide had heard from others who'd walked this road more times than he had. text: The country past Teginabad did what that country does, and Farrukh gave up early on the question of whether it had been described to him fairly, since it was not going to settle the argument either way and the mules had no opinion on it. What it had, in place of anything to look at, was stones, and the stones turned out to have been handled. The waymarkers stood at intervals a man on foot could keep in sight, each of them a stack about the height of a saddle, except that the third one was not. That one was new work, built low, and the stones along the top of it were small ones, the size a man picks up at the end of a day rather than the size he starts with; and the weathered faces, dark with however many summers, had been set inward, so that the whole stack showed its pale undersides to the road. There was something long lying in the drift beside it that he took at the time for more drift. A hundred paces on, at the stopping place, a dry stone windbreak had been patched along its lee with rock that had not come from anywhere within an hour's walk of it, and the wind had been at the dust behind that wall without finishing the job: hollows in the lee of it, softened at the rims and going shallow, not yet swept out flat. His guide's interest in stones extended to whether they were in the road.

text: They were in the lee of the next wall, eleven of them, sitting out the worst of the afternoon in the way of men who know exactly how long that lasts. They had been called up in the spring for the digging above the canal head - lawfully, by name, out of four villages - and kept past the season it had been called for, and then let go with their days counted and set against next year's assessment instead of coin, which the man doing the talking said twice over, not because Farrukh had missed it but because it still did not sound like a thing that could be true. They were walking home, which for a day and a half yet meant Farrukh's own road, at the pace of men in no hurry to arrive with nothing. What they wore was what a man digs in for a season and walks home in afterwards: one of them had a grain sack with a slit cut for his neck, and the rest had shoulders gone through where the basket rope had ridden. The wind came over the wall and they turned their backs into it without seeming to notice. Nothing they carried was worth his money, no claim of theirs touched him, and there was nothing at all they could make him do; and the oldest of them looked once at the bales on the mules and then away again, and stood there in the wind working out what a man in his position was entitled to say next.

text: The long thing in the drift a hundred paces back was the marker itself, a shaped stone the length of a man, out of its socket and half buried along its own length, and that was the whole explanation of the low new stack beside it. Four of them had been at the stone since first light and had got it as far as knee height twice; then they had built the stack out of loose rock instead, because a low stack is better than no stack for whoever comes next in a wind that takes the road away for a quarter of an hour at a time. What they wanted was the caravan's rope, and the guide, and Farrukh's own back, and an hour of the day, possibly two. The one who asked apologised for asking for hands rather than for goods, as though hands were the more expensive of the two, which in that heat, Farrukh thought, they were. Nobody would know the stone had been stood up. Nobody would know who had stood it. It would be of use only to people none of them would ever meet, arriving at that bend in weather none of them would be there for, and the caravan would be a day ahead of the eleven of them by tomorrow noon either way.

text: The watchpost sat on a rise off the last stretch, mudbrick, smaller than the word suggested, and one of the two men holding it came down to the road to meet the caravan and took his time walking back up again. He wanted the origin, the load, where bound - and then who was on the road behind them, and how many, and how they were travelling. He was entitled to the asking. He had nothing to write it on and nowhere to send it except down the line by whatever rider came next, and his own silver, he mentioned in the same tone he used for the road conditions, had not reached the post since before the summer, so that a man got his news the way he got everything else out here, which was late and from strangers. It was not a formality and it was not a threat. A party of men on foot with a season's days owed to them will be stopped further along and asked the same questions and counted, and their names will end up in a district's book, and probably nothing at all will come of it, and possibly next spring's summons will. Answering him would cost Farrukh one breath and nothing else in the world, which was, standing in the road with an unpaid man being polite to him, the whole of the difficulty.

One of them was walking home in a length newer than everything else he had on him, and when the party was stopped further along - it would be, this being the road for it - somebody would ask where it had come from, and the answer would be a caravan a day ahead with two mules and a hired guide. text: The gate fell behind him with the animals fed and the waterskins full, whatever that had cost. It was a small thing - a woman's asking price, met or shaved down by one dirham, nothing that would have troubled his father's ledgers for a moment - but it was the first arithmetic since Ghazni that Farrukh had done because he wanted to, and not because grief or custom or a customs officer's patience had required it of him. The desert road to Bost opened out ahead, indifferent to the distinction, the way roads are.
